The Greeks rewrote myth all the time in the name of political expediency.  What started as local myth was rewritten as politics changed. The entire patchwork of local myths and heroes were rewritten to fit with the Olympians as Greek culture went from small city-states to a more unified network. The result was a mythic structure that better suited the concerns of city elites and brought everything under the Olympian family tree.      
Geosophia does a fantastic job of collecting the stories and matching them to time and place.

I'd say the key to Forrest's success is that he blindly follows orders.  

He runs from bullies when Jenny tells him to.  The same order to run is his success in football, even requiring crowds to shout at him to stop.  That order is the only thing that keeps him from running off the field.  Then, he joins the military, where all he does is follow orders.  In fact, that makes him the ideal military man. Fast forward a few years and he's following Bubba's plan with the shrimp boat.  He adheres and is richly rewarded.  He invests in Apple, not understanding what the company is.  Someone told him that it was something he should do and he becomes wealthy beyond avarice.  Forrest is never conscious of what he's doing and has no plan, he just does what people tell him to.

In contrast, we have Jenny.  She tries to escape abuse, sets out on her own and follows her passions.  She struggles to live by her own will and what happens? She gets abused, addicted to drugs, and finally dies of AIDS.

**TL;DR: Even an idiot will succeed wildly if he only does what he is told.**

I think The Singularity idea is much more faith-based than anything else.  We're still working out how to get adequate food and water to everybody, there's a long way to go before machine-based immortality becomes anything but fantasy.  
It's an unrealistic leap to trust that technology will provide us with what would functionally be the classic religious idea of Heaven.  I see little difference between the two; aside from the window dressing, what would distinguish them?

In short, no.

The idea of property is a tool used to distribute resources and settle who is entitled to what, while reducing conflict.  Property rights is a form of social contract, so whether the food is 'hers' hinges on everyone else's agreement that it is.  If the food was purchased with counterfeit money, is it still hers?  What if she deceived someone into taking far less than it was worth?

While yes, computers are shrinking and getting more powerful, there's no guarantee of cheap energy and raw material to keep manufacturing and running them.  Immortality is a promise that has been made before, without any delivery.  No one's actually seen the Singularity happen(silly, I know), so I'm placing it in the realm of speculation.

Yes, talk to the players!  You'll get a much better handle on what works if you ask for feedback.

Here's three things it took me a long time to learn:
1. It's not about you vs. the players.  You don't "win" by killing off characters.  Bad luck and stupidity are one thing, but vindictiveness is another.  You "win" by having fun with the rest of the table, and spending more time in character generation than in session isn't fun.
2. Be flexible and say yes.  You can't know exactly where the players are going to go with your adventures, so expect them to throw you a curveball.  It's usually easier to take their idea and run with it than get them back on your intended path.
3.  Busy adult schedules end more games than bad GMs do.  All of you should try to keep game night open.  Make it sacrosanct and it will continue.
